title: First test render
ask: Give me a population density map of Texas… extruded… dramatic raytraced shadows… red-white-blue. Use real data, and real shadows.
what: An 800 px, 16-sample check of the pipeline: 317,903 Kontur hexagons became 2.2 million faces and path-traced in 8 seconds. Peaks were capped at 42 km and the base was light gray, so it read as flat and the white middle class blended into the base.

title: First full render
what: Peaks raised to 110 km and the sun lowered to 7.5° from the west-northwest so shadows run east across the state. Charcoal base, gray ground, gradient legend, title “Where 30 million people live”.

title: Brighter, taller, warmer, labeled
ask: Trim the scale so the zero point is a brighter red and the top is a brighter blue… boost the vertical scale… lighten and warm up the background… add annotation for the major city spikes.
what: Darkest ends of the ramp trimmed, peaks to 180 km, sand ground, and twelve cities with leader lines and peak densities. Labels anchor on the visible skyline (25th-tallest nearby cell) because the densest cell is an invisible needle.

title: Uninhabited land in red
ask: The gray near-zero population background of the map should be red too.
what: Kontur only lists inhabited hexagons, so empty land showed the base slab. The slab took the exact color of the lowest class.

title: Names only, five swatches
ask: Remove the density numbers… remove the leader lines… boost the vertical scale even more… simplify the legend into just 5 swatches.
what: Peaks to 280 km (2.5× the first render), plain names on each skyline, five swatches at 1, 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000+ people per km².

title: Plan oblique view
ask: Stretch the image vertically so the image is closer to the proportions of Texas as viewed top down, but keep the perspective view.
what: Blender renders with wide pixels (aspect 1/cos 50°): the ground keeps its top-down shape while heights still rise at the 50° view. Lighting is untouched and label positions come from Blender’s own camera projection.

title: Simpler title and a color grade
ask: Change the title to a simpler ‘Texas Population Density’… contrast, brightness, or other levels adjustments… bright and clean-looking.
what: Levels put the sand near white, a gentle S-curve kept shadows strong, grays were neutralized, and reds pulled back from neon. Legend swatches are rendered as flat tiles under the map’s lighting so they match after the grade.

title: Readable labels and a stepped legend
ask: The place labels need adjustment so they’re a bit easier to read. Also the scale needs an extra callout… or make each swatch a different height.
what: Bold names on cream pills with a faint outline and shadow. The swatches rise one step per 10×, with callouts: darkest blue is 10,000× denser than darkest red, and heights are linear (the tallest spike’s real value is printed).

title: 2026 Senate results draped on population
ask: Source county level election results from the 2026 Texas US Senate race and drape those colors on the population map instead of coloring by density.
what: 254-county results (Wikipedia, spot-checked against Decision Desk HQ and the Dallas Morning News). Each hexagon takes its county’s two-party margin; uninhabited land is neutral gray.

title: County-colored land
ask: In this case I would color the slab according the county election results, too.
what: The land slab is built from the 254 Census county polygons, each in its result color, so empty counties read correctly and spikes show where the votes are.

title: Precinct-level 2024 results
ask: Search the web for better resolution results, like at the precinct level… you can probably find it for the 2024 presidential results.
what: 2026 precinct data is not yet published statewide, so this uses the NYT’s 9,718 Texas precincts for 2024 (totals within 0.1% of certified). Cities split into blue cores and red suburbs; the Rio Grande Valley shows the 2024 shift.

title: Sun at 15°, centered labels
ask: Your city labels aren't correctly centered in their white background pill shapes… bring [the light] up higher above the horizon, try 15º.
what: Names are centered on cap height. Shadows are half as long. The grade now measures the bare ground in each render, so the background stays the same cream at any sun angle.
